WORLD CLOCK & DAYLIGHT · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

What time is it there — and are they awake?

Pick the cities you actually care about and see them side by side: current local time, sunrise, sunset, how long the day is, and a plain waking-hours label so you know whether a call is a kindness or an alarm clock.

Nothing is uploaded and there is no network request at all. Sunrise and sunset are computed here, in this tab, from the US Naval Observatory's published almanac algorithm.

Your cities

Updates every second. Sunrise and sunset are for each city's own local calendar day.
City Local time Now Sunrise Sunset Daylight vs. you Remove

No cities selected. Add one below, or .

Add a city

What's computed, and how accurate it is

ValueHow
Local timeYour browser's own IANA time zone database, so daylight saving is already handled for every city
Sunrise / sunsetThe Sunrise/Sunset Algorithm from the Almanac for Computers, 1990 (Nautical Almanac Office, US Naval Observatory), using city-centre coordinates — accurate to roughly a minute outside the polar circles
Daylight lengthThe interval between the two, for that city's own local calendar day
Waking-hours labelA courtesy heuristic on the local clock alone: asleep before 07:00 and from 22:00, early to 09:00, working hours to 17:00, evening to 22:00
vs. youThe difference between each city's current UTC offset and your own, so half-hour and three-quarter-hour zones read correctly

The waking-hours label knows nothing about weekends, public holidays, shift work, or the person's actual job. It is a nudge before you dial, not a fact about them.

Common questions

How are sunrise and sunset calculated without a network call?

From the Sunrise/Sunset Algorithm published in the Almanac for Computers, 1990 (Nautical Almanac Office, United States Naval Observatory) — the public-domain algorithm behind most open-source sunrise calculators. It needs only a date, a latitude and a longitude, all of which are already on this page, so the whole computation runs in your browser. It is accurate to roughly a minute outside the polar circles.

Why does the daylight length differ slightly from my weather app?

Three ordinary reasons. The almanac algorithm is accurate to about a minute, not to the second. This tool uses city-centre coordinates, and sunrise genuinely differs across a large metropolitan area. And published times sometimes measure a slightly different event — the sun's upper limb clearing a flat horizon versus the centre of the disc — which shifts the answer by a minute or two. None of these matter for knowing whether it is light there; none of them should be relied on for navigation, aviation, or religious observance.

What do the Asleep, Early, Working hours and Evening labels mean?

They are a plain courtesy heuristic about waking hours based only on the local clock: asleep before 07:00 and from 22:00, early until 09:00, working hours until 17:00, evening until 22:00. They are not a claim about anyone's actual schedule, working week, or public holidays, and they do not know about weekends. Treat them as a nudge before you call, not as a fact about the person.

Is anything uploaded or tracked?

No. There is no account, no cookie, no analytics vendor and no network request of any kind — the page ships the city list and the solar maths and computes everything locally. The cities you pick are remembered in your own browser's local storage so the page opens the same way next time, and anonymous feature counters are kept in the same place. Both can be cleared with the button in the footer, and Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Can I share my set of cities with someone?

Yes. The Copy share link button puts the current selection into the URL, so the person you send it to opens the same cities in the same order. The link carries nothing but the city names — no identifier, and nothing about you.

How is this different from my phone's built-in world clock?

A phone's world clock shows the time in a city; it usually does not show sunrise, sunset, daylight length, or whether that time is a reasonable one to call. See this tool vs. your phone's built-in world clock for the comparison.

Why is India's time zone UTC+5:30 instead of a whole number?

Because Indian Standard Time is anchored to a meridian near the country's geographic centre rather than rounded to the nearest hour, and the country has run on one national clock since 1906 despite spanning roughly two hours of longitude. See why India's time zone is UTC+5:30 for the full explanation, including the other half-hour and 45-minute zones around the world.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. Sunrise and sunset are computed from a published almanac approximation using city-centre coordinates and are accurate to roughly a minute in ordinary latitudes — they are not suitable for navigation, aviation, maritime use, religious observance, or any purpose where an exact solar time matters. The waking-hours labels are a courtesy heuristic and say nothing about any individual's real schedule. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you enter, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record.

Everything runs in your browser. Nothing you do here is ever uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Your selected cities and anonymous feature events (city_added, city_removed, link_copied, sorted_by_time) are kept only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Also worth a pass on the same repo: Cron DST Drift Check catches the schedule that skips or double-fires across a daylight-saving transition — the same time-zone arithmetic, applied to the jobs that run while you sleep.

Also: World Traveler, a Garmin watch face that shows 42 world cities on a 24-hour ring.

Free and open source. If this saved you a badly-timed phone call, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-your-phones-clock-app.html.text:
← back to the world clock

This tool vs. your phone's built-in world clock

A phone's world clock is built for one question: what time is it there. It answers that well, one city and one row at a time. It is usually not built to answer the question that actually decides whether to call someone -- is this a reasonable time for them, or the middle of their night.

What each one is for

Your phone's world clock is fast, always in your pocket, and fine for the one or two cities you check constantly, especially as a lock-screen widget. It shows a time. Working out whether that time is a good one to call still happens in your head.

This tool shows current local time, sunrise, sunset, daylight length, and a plain waking-hours label (Asleep, Early, Working hours, Evening) for every city you pick, side by side in one table -- so the "is this a good time" judgment is answered on the screen, not left for you to do from the clock digits alone.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What time is it in one city I check constantly?A phone's world clock or lock-screen widget is faster for this.
Is now a reasonable time to call several people in different cities?This tool's waking-hours label answers it for every city at once, without mental math.
When does the sun rise or set there, and how long is the day?Not shown by most phone clock apps. Computed here from a public-domain almanac algorithm.
Can I send someone my exact city list, live rather than a screenshot?This tool's Copy share link button -- a phone widget can only be screenshotted.
Is anything uploaded or tracked?No. Nothing leaves your browser; there is no account, upload, or network request.

Common questions

Doesn't my phone already have a world clock?

Yes, and it is fine at the one job it does: showing the current time in a city you added. What it typically does not show is sunrise, sunset, daylight length, or any indication of whether that time is a reasonable one to call — you still have to do that math in your head from the clock digits alone.

What does this add that a phone clock app doesn't?

Sunrise, sunset, and daylight length for each city, computed from the same public-domain almanac algorithm regardless of platform, plus a plain waking-hours label (Asleep, Early, Working hours, Evening) so you can tell at a glance whether it is a kind time to call — not just what the clock reads. All of it is visible for every city at once, in one table, rather than one screen per city.

Can I share my list of cities the way I could screenshot a phone widget?

Yes, and more usefully: the Copy share link button puts your exact city selection into a URL. The person you send it to opens the same cities in the same order, live and current — not a screenshot that goes stale the moment the clock ticks forward.

Does this replace my phone's world clock?

Not necessarily — a phone's world clock is still the faster glance for a city or two you check constantly, especially from a lock screen or widget. This tool is built for the case a phone clock handles poorly: several cities at once, with enough context to actually decide when to call, not just what the local time is.

Is anything uploaded or tracked?

No. The tool this page links to runs entirely in your browser, with no account, no upload, and no network request of any kind.

No warranty. This page and the linked tool compute sunrise, sunset, and daylight length from a published almanac approximation using city-centre coordinates; they are not suitable for navigation, aviation, maritime use, or religious observance, and the waking-hours labels are a courtesy heuristic, not a claim about any individual's real schedule. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. The tool this page links to runs entirely client-side, with no account, no upload, and no network request of any kind.

Nothing here says or implies that your phone's built-in world clock is bad at its job — it is a different job: a fast glance at one city's time, where this tool adds the context for several cities at once.

why-is-indias-time-zone-utc-5-30.html.text:
← World Clock & Daylight

Why is India's time zone UTC+5:30, not a whole number?

Most of the world rounds its clocks to the nearest whole hour from UTC. India doesn't: Indian Standard Time is exactly five and a half hours ahead. It isn't a rounding quirk or a historical accident that stuck — it's a deliberate choice, and this world clock renders it correctly wherever it shows up, including the "vs. you" column when you're comparing your own zone against it.

Open Mumbai and New Delhi on the world clock

The reasoning behind 5:30

India Standard Time is anchored to 82.5°E — the meridian passing near Mirzapur, close to the country's geographic centre. Solar noon on that line falls almost exactly 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of solar noon at Greenwich. Rounding to a flat UTC+5 or UTC+6 would have made the clock read noticeably early or late against the sun for whichever coast was rounded away from; UTC+5:30 was chosen to split that difference rather than accept it on one side.

One clock for two hours of longitude

India stretches from about 68°E to 97°E — roughly two hours of solar time from its western border to its eastern one. Before 1906 the country ran two zones, Bombay Time and Calcutta Time; they were merged into one Indian Standard Time that year, and the country has kept a single zone since independence for the sake of one national timetable — one clock for trains, broadcasting and government offices, rather than a traveller crossing an internal time boundary.

The tradeoff is real and it's visible on this tool's own city list, which carries both ends of the country. Mumbai, in the west, and New Delhi are close enough in longitude that the difference barely registers — but the far northeast, near the Myanmar border, sees the sun rise nearly two hours before it does in the west. A single national clock means the northeast starts its working day in bright daylight while clocks nationwide still read the same 5:30 offset.

CityTime zoneUTC offset
MumbaiAsia/KolkataUTC+5:30
New DelhiAsia/KolkataUTC+5:30

Both cities share the same IANA zone, Asia/Kolkata, and this world clock reads it straight from your browser's own time zone database — the same source used for every city on the list — so the half-hour offset, and the "vs. you" comparison against it, are exact rather than approximated.

India isn't alone

Half-hour and other fractional offsets show up wherever a government has favoured tracking the sun over rounding to a clean number:

PlaceOffset
IranUTC+3:30
AfghanistanUTC+4:30
India, Sri LankaUTC+5:30
MyanmarUTC+6:30
NepalUTC+5:45
Newfoundland, CanadaUTC-3:30

Nepal's UTC+5:45 is one of only two 45-minute offsets used anywhere in the world. None of these are mistakes to round away — a tool that assumes every zone sits on a whole hour will misreport the local time in any of them.

Common questions

Why does India use a half-hour offset instead of a whole one?

India Standard Time is fixed to 82.5°E longitude, roughly the meridian running through Mirzapur, near the geographic middle of the country. Solar noon there falls almost exactly 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of solar noon at Greenwich, so the government set the clock to UTC+5:30 rather than round to the nearest whole hour, which would have pushed one coast's solar time further from the clock than the other's.

Why does a country spanning two hours of longitude use only one time zone?

India used two time zones, Bombay Time and Calcutta Time, until they were unified into a single Indian Standard Time in 1906, and the country has kept one zone since independence for administrative simplicity — one national timetable for trains, broadcasting and government offices. The tradeoff is real: solar noon in the far east (near the Myanmar border) arrives roughly two hours earlier than solar noon in the far west (near the Pakistan border), so a single clock reads noon well after sunrise in the east and well before it in the west.

Is India the only country with a half-hour or unusual time zone offset?

No. Iran and Afghanistan use UTC+3:30 and UTC+4:30. Sri Lanka and Myanmar use UTC+5:30 and UTC+6:30. Nepal uses UTC+5:45, one of only two 45-minute offsets in the world. Newfoundland, Canada runs UTC-3:30. None of these are errors — each was chosen so the local clock tracks solar time more closely than the nearest whole-hour zone would.
